findings.claim: The exam tip and practice question 6 both teach a 12-mark evaluation worth '[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]'.
findings.truth: The UK paper is 1 hour, 60 marks including 3 for SPaG, 30% of the GCSE, with compulsory questions on all three themes and a separate Resource Booklet. Question tariffs run 1-8 marks; there is no 12-mark question and no 12+3 form. The spec's 'maximum of 12 marks plus SPaG' sentence describes the extended response ceiling across components and is reached on the geographical skills paper, not this one. Every 12-mark practice question and every exam tip naming 12 marks was retariffed to 8 marks plus 3 SPaG.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section (forms of assessment; SPaG 3 marks per component) plus the task brief's tariff ruling

findings.claim: 'The Pennines ... run as a granite and limestone spine through northern England because these rocks resist weathering more than the softer Carboniferous rocks of the surrounding lowlands.'
findings.truth: The Pennines have no granite at the surface. They are Carboniferous limestone overlain by Millstone Grit, so the sentence also contradicts itself by contrasting the ridge with 'softer Carboniferous rocks'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Pennines (geology): 'Each of the structures consists of Carboniferous limestone overlain with Millstone Grit.'

findings.claim: 'High Force has retreated several kilometres from its original position downstream of Middleton-in-Teesdale' (repeated in the 4-mark mark scheme).
findings.truth: The gorge below High Force is about 700 m long, which is the measure of its retreat. High Force is upstream of Middleton-in-Teesdale, not downstream of it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, High Force: 'The length of the gorge is currently about 700 metres.'

findings.claim: 'High Force as a 22-metre waterfall'; 'the synoptic skills paper rewards locational detail'.
findings.truth: High Force drops 21 m. Synoptic assessment sits in the geographical skills paper, so it cannot be the reason for losing marks on this paper.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, High Force ('total height 21 m'); spec section on synoptic assessment

findings.claim: 'The Old Man of Hoy off Orkney is a UK example of this sequence in basalt.'
findings.truth: The Old Man of Hoy is an Old Red Sandstone stack standing on a plinth of basalt. The stack itself is sandstone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Old Man of Hoy: 'a red sandstone stack, perched on a plinth of basalt rock'.

findings.claim: 'OCR mark schemes reward the chain of cause and effect' (same pattern in L6 'OCR examiners specifically reward balanced evaluations' and L8 'OCR mark schemes reward case-study specificity').
findings.truth: These are invented claims about board mark schemes. Rewritten in house vocabulary as what earns credit.
findings.evidence: house rule on copyright distancing; no such wording exists in the spec

findings.claim: 'the Commonwealth (54 countries...)', repeated in a 4-mark mark scheme and as the correct option of a knowledge check.
findings.truth: The Commonwealth has had 56 members since Togo and Gabon joined in 2022.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Commonwealth of Nations: 56 member states.

findings.claim: 'Heathrow connects to more international cities than any other European airport' (repeated in a flashcard answer).
findings.truth: Heathrow is not the European airport serving the most destinations; Frankfurt and Paris both serve more. Heathrow does link the UK to more than 80 countries and is one of Europe's busiest airports.
findings.evidence: Heathrow's own destination count (over 200 destinations in more than 80 countries)

findings.claim: 'Cultural exports (music, film, sport, fashion) generate £100 billion a year.'
findings.truth: £100bn+ is the creative industries' contribution to the UK economy. Creative-industry exports are roughly half that, so the claim conflates output with exports.
findings.evidence: DCMS creative industries GVA (£124bn, 2023) versus creative services exports

findings.claim: 'Net migration in 2023 was around 685,000 — a record figure' (also in a 4-mark mark scheme and a flashcard; the same claim runs through L6).
findings.truth: 685,000 was the first provisional estimate for the year to December 2023 and has been revised up. ONS now puts the record at 944,000 in the year to March 2023; net migration was 204,000 in the year to June 2025.
findings.evidence: ONS long-term international migration bulletin, year ending June 2025: 'the peak in YE March 2023 (944,000)'.

findings.claim: 'A child born in the South East today can expect to live four years longer, earn 50% more and be twice as likely to attend university as one born in the North East.'
findings.truth: All three figures overstate the gap: life expectancy differs by about three years, median full-time pay by about a fifth, and higher-education entry is not double. The direction is right, so the sentence was rewritten without the invented precision.
findings.evidence: ONS regional life expectancy and ASHE median pay (direction confirmed, exact values not asserted)

findings.claim: 'Coal employment fell from 100,000 in 1980 to under 200 today' (repeated in a flashcard framed as UK employment and in a 6-mark mark scheme).
findings.truth: UK coal mining employed 247,000 people in 1976 and about 360 in 2022. 100,000 in 1980 is far too low for the UK figure the flashcard asks for.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Coal mining in the United Kingdom: employment 1976 = 247,000; 2022 = 360.

findings.claim: 'Targeted policies (HS2 northern phases, Northern Powerhouse, freeports) aim to break this cycle.'
findings.truth: The northern leg of HS2 was cancelled in October 2023, so it cannot be cited as a live levelling-up policy.
findings.evidence: UK government cancellation of HS2 Phase 2, October 2023

findings.claim: 'The UK's population stood at around 67.6 million in 2024' (repeated in a flashcard; L9 says 67 million).
findings.truth: The ONS mid-2024 estimate is 69.28 million. 67.6 million is the mid-2022 figure.
findings.evidence: ONS mid-year estimates via Wikipedia, Demography of the United Kingdom: 2024 = 69,281,437.

findings.claim: 'Net migration to the UK reached a record 685,000 in 2023' (content, key fact, flashcard and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: Same as F10: the ONS record is 944,000 in the year to March 2023.
findings.evidence: ONS long-term international migration bulletin, year ending June 2025

findings.claim: 'Manchester now operates a Clean Air Zone covering buses, taxis and HGVs to address NO2 levels' (repeated in a key fact, the conclusion, a knowledge check pair and an 8-mark mark scheme).
findings.truth: The Greater Manchester Clean Air Zone was never introduced. It was paused in 2022 and remains under review; the city works to an investment-led clean air plan instead. Bath, Birmingham, Bradford, Bristol, Newcastle, Portsmouth and Sheffield operate charging zones.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Clean Air Zone: Greater Manchester listed under 'Planned or suspended', 'Under review'.

findings.claim: '60% renewable electricity by 2030' given as Manchester's sustainability target (content, revision collapsible, flashcard, mark scheme; repeated in L10).
findings.truth: Manchester has no such target. Its published targets are a science-based carbon budget agreed with the Tyndall Centre and a cut of at least 50% in direct CO2 emissions between 2020 and 2025.
findings.evidence: manchesterclimate.com/targets: 'reduce our direct CO2 emissions by at least 50% between 2020-25'; carbon budget of 15 Mt CO2 from 2018.

findings.claim: '43,000 properties lost power; one person died' (repeated in a 6-mark mark scheme).
findings.truth: About 46,300 properties lost power during Storm Desmond, and three deaths were attributed to the storm.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Storm Desmond: 46,300 properties without power; three casualties.

findings.claim: 'Hornsea Two off Yorkshire is the world's second-largest offshore wind farm' (repeated as a flashcard question in L10).
findings.truth: Hornsea 2 overtook Hornsea 1 in August 2022 to become the world's largest offshore wind farm. Hornsea 3 will overtake it when built.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Hornsea Wind Farm: 'Hornsea Project 2 overtook Hornsea One as the largest offshore wind farm in the world'.

findings.claim: 'Kielder Water ... supplies the North East and East Midlands' (repeated in a key fact).
findings.truth: Kielder supplies the North East only, releasing water to the Tyne and transferring it to the Wear and Tees. It does not supply the East Midlands.
findings.evidence: Kielder Transfer Scheme (Tyne-Wear-Tees), Northumbrian Water

findings.claim: 'The Lake District's reservoirs (Haweswater, Thirlmere) feed Manchester, 100 km away, through pipelines built in the 19th century' (flashcard asks which Manchester reservoirs were built in the 19th century).
findings.truth: The Thirlmere aqueduct opened in 1894, but Haweswater dam dates from the 1930s and its aqueduct from the 1950s. The route is over 150 km.
findings.evidence: Thirlmere Aqueduct (1894); Haweswater Reservoir (dam completed 1935)

findings.claim: 'Ely Ouse-Essex transfer moves water 100 km' in the 8-mark mark scheme.
findings.truth: The transfer runs roughly 30 km from the Ely Ouse at Denver to the Stour and Blackwater. The distance figure was removed rather than replaced.
findings.evidence: Ely Ouse to Essex Transfer Scheme, Environment Agency / Essex & Suffolk Water

findings.claim: 'deliver these supplies for 67 million people'.
findings.truth: The UK population is about 69.3 million (ONS mid-2024).
findings.evidence: ONS mid-2024 estimate, 69,281,437

findings.claim: 'the planned 2035 ban on new combustion-engine cars' (repeated in a flashcard and an 8-mark mark scheme).
findings.truth: The UK phase-out date for new pure petrol and diesel cars is 2030. The 2035 date was set in 2023 and then reversed.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK consultation: 'the UK government's commitment to phase out pure petrol and diesel cars by 2030'.

findings.claim: 'UK electricity in 2024 came from renewables (~50% combined), gas (~30%), nuclear (~14%) and biomass (~5%)' (repeated in the conclusion, a knowledge check option and an 8-mark mark scheme).
findings.truth: The list double-counts biomass, which is already inside the renewables total, and leaves no room for imports. The 2024 mix was renewables 45% (wind 29.7, solar 6.5, biomass 6.9, hydro 1.6), gas 26.8%, nuclear 11.8%, net imports 15.1%.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Electricity sector in the United Kingdom, 2024 generation mix: 'Renewables ... supplied 45% of generation'.

findings.claim: 'Manchester aims for 60% renewable electricity by 2030.'
findings.truth: Same invented target as F20; replaced with Manchester's science-based carbon budget.
findings.evidence: manchesterclimate.com/targets

findings.claim: Flashcard question 'What is the world's second-largest offshore wind farm, off the UK coast?'
findings.truth: Hornsea 2 was the world's largest when it opened in 2022.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Hornsea Wind Farm

findings.claim: 'About 40% of NHS beds are occupied by patients over 65' (content, key fact and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: The widely published NHS figure is that people over 65 use roughly two-thirds of hospital bed days; 40% is closer to their share of admissions. Options: (a) change all four places to 'about two-thirds of hospital bed days', (b) leave as an admissions figure by rewording to 'about 40% of hospital admissions', or (c) leave. Recommend (b): it is the smallest change that makes the sentence true.
findings.evidence: NHS England / Age UK bed-day statistics; could not be fetched inside the source budget
findings.ruling: Leave: spec citation kept / figure unverified this session.

findings.claim: 'Around 17% of NHS doctors and 15% of NHS nurses were trained outside the UK' (also a knowledge check stem and a flashcard).
findings.truth: Both figures look far too low: roughly a third of doctors on the GMC register qualified outside the UK, and about a quarter of NHS nurses in England hold a non-British nationality. Recommend raising to about one third of doctors and about one quarter of nurses once a source can be opened, since the knowledge check stem teaches the number directly.
findings.evidence: GMC register and House of Commons Library briefing CBP-7783 (returned 403 to the fetch)
findings.ruling: Leave: spec citation kept / figure unverified this session.

findings.claim: 'men in Blackpool die on average nine years earlier than men in Westminster' (exam tip, 4-mark mark scheme and flashcard use the same nine-year gap).
findings.truth: ONS local-authority life expectancy puts Blackpool males near 73 and Westminster males near 85, a gap closer to eleven years. The claim understates rather than overstates, so it costs no marks. Recommend changing all four places to 'about eleven years' once the ONS table can be opened.
findings.evidence: ONS life expectancy for local areas of the UK; page not reachable in this session
findings.ruling: Leave: spec citation kept / figure unverified this session.

findings.claim: 'the soft boulder-clay cliffs of Holderness ... strip back the coastline by up to two metres a year'; the L3 flashcard calls two metres the average rate.
findings.truth: The usual published figure is an average of about 1.8 m a year with local maxima nearer 4 m, so 'up to two metres' reads as a maximum when it is really the average.
findings.evidence: standard Holderness erosion figures

findings.claim: 'Around 19% of the UK population is now over 65, up from 13% in 1980.'
findings.truth: The 65-and-over share was about 15% in 1981; 13% is closer to 1971.
findings.evidence: ONS population by age

findings.claim: '341.4 mm ... more than the average monthly rainfall for the whole of December'.
findings.truth: True against the UK December average but not against Honister's own December average, which is itself 350-450 mm.
findings.evidence: Met Office Honister/Seathwaite rainfall averages

findings.claim: 'Total economic damage exceeded £500 million'.
findings.truth: Not wrong, but understated: the published estimate for Storm Desmond is at least £870 million.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Storm Desmond

findings.claim: 'Heavy rainfall events have intensified by about 4% per decade since 1961.'
findings.truth: Could not be matched to any Met Office State of the UK Climate statement; the published framing is a percentage increase in rainfall from extremely wet days since 1961.
findings.evidence: Met Office State of the UK Climate

findings.claim: 'Cultural assets like the Royal Exchange theatre, HOME and Whitworth Park'.
findings.truth: The cultural asset is the Whitworth art gallery; Whitworth Park is the park around it.
findings.evidence: the Whitworth, University of Manchester

findings.claim: 'pollinator populations halved since 1980' (repeated in a 4-mark mark scheme and a flashcard).
findings.truth: Published UK work reports about a third of pollinator species declining in distribution between 1980 and 2013, not a halving of populations.
findings.evidence: UK pollinator distribution studies

findings.claim: 'the Sihwa-style Swansea Bay Tidal Lagoon is paused'.
findings.truth: Swansea Bay was a tidal lagoon proposal, not a barrage like Sihwa, and it was rejected by the UK government in 2018 rather than paused.
findings.evidence: Swansea Bay Tidal Lagoon decision, June 2018

summary: No lesson is clean: all ten teach a 12-mark evaluation question that this 60-mark, one-hour UK paper does not set, so every practice question 6 and exam tip was retariffed to 8 marks plus 3 SPaG. Beyond that the unit carries four hard factual errors that would mislead a student in a case study answer (Pennines granite, the Old Man of Hoy in basalt, a Greater Manchester Clean Air Zone that was never introduced, and an invented Manchester 60% renewable electricity target), plus a run of stale national statistics (net migration, UK population, the 2024 energy mix, the petrol and diesel phase-out year, Commonwealth membership and UK coal employment).
